summary: Mem0 is the most widely adopted memory layer for AI agents as of August 2026: an Apache-2.0 open-source library (~62.8k GitHub stars, ~7.3k forks) plus a hosted platform that extracts salient facts from conversations with an LLM, stores them in vector (and optionally graph) stores, and retrieves compact relevant memories at query time instead of replaying full conversation history. It raised a $24M combined seed + Series A (announced Oct 2025, led by Basis Set Ventures with Kindred Ventures, Peak XV, GitHub Fund, and Y Combinator), and third-party 2026 landscape reports describe it as the memory provider for AWS's Agent SDK with AWS-native backends (Neptune Analytics, ElastiCache for Valkey) and ~21 framework integrations. Its market position rests heavily on benchmark marketing (LoCoMo/LongMemEval) that has been publicly and credibly disputed by competitors, and notably its own paper shows a full-context baseline outscoring Mem0 on LoCoMo.
architecture: WRITE PATH (per the paper, arXiv 2504.19413): a two-phase LLM pipeline. Extraction phase: for each new user-assistant message pair, an LLM (GPT-4o-mini in the paper) receives a prompt P = (asynchronously maintained global conversation summary S, the last m=10 messages, the new message pair) and extracts a set of candidate salient memories (atomic facts). Update phase: for each candidate fact, the system retrieves the top s=10 semantically similar existing memories via dense vector embeddings, then an LLM tool-call decides one of four operations — ADD (no semantic equivalent exists), UPDATE (augment an existing memory), DELETE (new info contradicts a stored memory), NOOP — and a resolver executes it. STORAGE: memories live as embedded text records in a pluggable vector store (Qdrant et al.) scoped by user/agent/session IDs with metadata, plus a history store; the graph variant Mem0-g additionally extracts entity-relation triplets into a graph DB (Neo4j-class stores; AWS Neptune Analytics support added Sept 2025). READ PATH: the query is embedded and run through vector similarity search filtered by user/agent/run IDs; ranked top-k memories are returned and injected into the agent's prompt (Mem0-g adds graph/entity traversal for relational queries). NOTE — ARCHITECTURE HAS DRIFTED: the platform's "April 2026 algorithm" (mem0.ai/research) describes "ADD-only extraction" (append-only writes, ~2x faster, no synchronous UPDATE/DELETE), hierarchical fact extraction, write-time temporal classification, asynchronous fire-and-forget memory decay/consolidation (sold as "Dream" on the Pro tier), and retrieval fusing three parallel signals: semantic, keyword, and entity. The current docs confirm the append-only model ("new memories are added without overwriting or deleting existing memories") with conflict handling pushed to retrieval-time ranking and async consolidation — so the shipping product no longer matches the ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP design the paper benchmarked.
token_strategy: Mem0's pitch is substitution: instead of sending the full conversation history to the answering model, send only retrieved atomic facts. Paper numbers (vendor-measured): full raw conversations in LoCoMo average ~26,000 tokens, Mem0's memory representation ~7,000 tokens per conversation (~14,000 for Mem0-g), yielding the marketed ">90% token savings vs full-context" and a 91% p95 latency reduction (total p95 1.44s vs 17.12s for full-context). The README/marketing trio is "+26% accuracy vs OpenAI Memory, 91% faster, 90% fewer tokens." The 2026 research page restates this more modestly as ~6,900 tokens per retrieval call vs 25,000+ full-context, framed as "3-4x lower token cost." Important caveats: the baseline is always full-context stuffing (the most token-expensive possible baseline), not conventional RAG, which in their own paper uses comparable or fewer tokens; and the 26% accuracy figure is relative to OpenAI's memory feature (J=52.90), not the strongest baseline. Write-side token costs (LLM calls for extraction and, historically, update decisions on every add) are real but not included in the savings framing; the 2026 shift to ADD-only extraction implicitly acknowledges this write amplification.

benchmarks.claim: Mem0 overall J=66.88 (single-hop 67.13, multi-hop 51.15, open-domain 72.93, temporal 55.51); Mem0-g overall J=68.44 (single-hop 65.71, multi-hop 47.19, open-domain 75.71, temporal 58.13). Baselines: full-context 72.90, Zep 65.99, best RAG 60.97, LangMem 58.10, OpenAI Memory 52.90, A-Mem 48.38. Marketed as '26% relative improvement over OpenAI'.
benchmarks.source: https://arxiv.org/html/2504.19413v1 (verified directly against the paper's tables)
benchmarks.caveats: Full-context beats both Mem0 variants on overall J in Mem0's own paper; the headline 26% is vs OpenAI Memory, one of the weakest baselines. All numbers vendor-run with GPT-4o-mini.

benchmarks.claim: Mem0 total latency p50/p95 = 0.708s/1.440s vs full-context 9.87s/17.12s (91% p95 reduction); ~7K tokens per conversation vs ~26K full-context (>90% savings); Zep measured at >600K tokens.
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor-measured; Zep disputes its own latency figure, saying Mem0 ran Zep searches sequentially instead of in parallel.

benchmarks.claim: 92.5 overall (single-hop 94.6, multi-hop 95.4, open-domain 82.3, temporal 92.5), ~6.7-7.0K tokens, p50 latency 0.88-1.09s.
benchmarks.caveats: Self-reported, platform-only (README says OSS users should expect only 'directionally similar' results); no independent verification found; third-party roundups report materially different scores when independently re-run — one comparison cites a 45.4-point gap between a vendor figure and an independent measurement of the same benchmark.

benchmarks.claim: LongMemEval 94.4 (with claimed 98.2% assistant-recall), BEAM at 1M tokens: 64.1.
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor-reported only; BEAM is not yet a widely independently replicated benchmark; no third-party reproduction located.

benchmarks.claim: Zep says a properly configured Zep scores J=75.14 (+/-0.17), ~10% above Mem0's best paper score (68.44), vs the 65.99 Mem0 reported for Zep; and Zep search p95 of 0.632s vs Mem0's reported 0.778s.
benchmarks.caveats: This is also a vendor claim from a direct competitor; Mem0 in turn has published corrections of Zep's earlier 84% LoCoMo claim (arguing Zep included excluded adversarial categories, giving 58.44%). Neither side's numbers have neutral third-party adjudication.

pricing: Hosted platform tiers (mem0.ai/pricing, Aug 2026): Hobby — free, 10,000 add requests/mo, 1,000 retrieval requests/mo, 1 project, unlimited end users, community support. Starter — $19/mo, 50,000 adds/mo, 5,000 retrievals/mo, 1 project. Pro — $249/mo, 500,000 adds/mo, 50,000 retrievals/mo, unlimited projects, advanced analytics, graph memory (entity linking), "Dream" memory consolidation, private Slack support. Enterprise — custom: unlimited requests, SLA support, on-prem deployment, audit logs, SSO, custom integrations. Usage-based pricing is offered for traffic that doesn't fit fixed tiers. The open-source library is free (Apache 2.0) with bring-your-own LLM/vector-store costs. Funding: $24M combined seed + Series A announced October 2025, led by Basis Set Ventures, with Kindred Ventures (seed lead), Peak XV Partners, GitHub Fund, Y Combinator, and angels including Scott Belsky, Dharmesh Shah, Olivier Pomel (Datadog), Paul Copplestone (Supabase), and Thomas Dohmke (ex-GitHub).
weaknesses: In Mem0's own paper, the trivial full-context baseline outscores Mem0 on LoCoMo overall (J=72.90 vs 66.88/68.44), so the specialized memory system loses to just pasting the whole conversation whenever it fits in context; the marketed '26% improvement' is against OpenAI Memory, one of the weakest baselines tested.

Public benchmark-methodology dispute with Zep: Zep alleges Mem0 misconfigured its evaluation (assigned the user role to both speakers in Zep's user graph, embedded timestamps in message text instead of Zep's created_at field breaking temporal reasoning, and ran searches sequentially, inflating Zep's latency), and claims a corrected Zep score of J=75.14 — above Mem0's best. Mem0 has counter-attacked Zep's own 84% claim (arguing it becomes 58.44% under the benchmark's spec). Neither side is independently adjudicated.

The LoCoMo benchmark both companies fight over is itself weak for this purpose (criticism from Zep and Letta): conversations average only ~16K-26K tokens (fits in any modern context window), category-5 data is unusable, speaker attribution errors and ambiguous questions exist, and it doesn't test knowledge updates over time — so it under-stresses exactly what memory systems claim to do.

The impressive 2026 numbers (LoCoMo 92.5, LongMemEval 94.4) are self-reported, apply to the closed managed platform rather than the open-source library (README: OSS gets only 'directionally similar' results), and are not reproducible from the published paper, whose architecture (ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP) the platform has since abandoned for ADD-only extraction with async decay — meaning the peer-visible paper no longer describes the shipping product.

Fact-extraction is lossy by construction: practitioners report it stores explicit atomic statements and struggles with nuance, implicit behavioral patterns, and information whose relevance is only apparent later; extraction quality also depends entirely on the underlying LLM used.

Write amplification: every memory add historically required multiple LLM calls (extraction plus per-fact update decisions), a cost and latency the token-savings marketing excludes; the 2026 'ADD-only, 2x faster extraction' change is an implicit admission. The docs also note the append-only model can create duplicate memories (e.g., with inconsistent infer=False usage).

Token-savings framing compares only against full-context stuffing, the most expensive possible baseline, not against conventional RAG, which in Mem0's own paper achieves competitive scores at comparable token budgets.

summary: Zep (YC W24, founded 2023 by Daniel Chalef) is a managed "agent memory / context engineering" platform built on Graphiti, its Apache-2.0 open-source temporal knowledge graph engine (~29.7k GitHub stars as of Aug 2026). Its differentiator versus vector-store memory products is a bi-temporal knowledge graph: facts are extracted as entity-relationship-entity edges with explicit validity windows, and contradicted facts are invalidated (dated) rather than deleted, so the graph can answer "what was true when." Positioning is enterprise-focused ("agent memory infrastructure for the enterprise", SOC 2, HIPAA BAA tier), with homepage claims of 1.4M+ active context graphs and sub-200ms p95 retrieval, and named customers including Samsung, Zscaler, Twin Health, and HoneyBook (vendor claims, not independently verified). It is in an open, unresolved benchmark war with Mem0 over LoCoMo methodology, and its own headline numbers (DMR 94.8%, LongMemEval +18.5%) are self-reported in a non-peer-reviewed arXiv preprint.
architecture: WRITE PATH (Graphiti engine): Data arrives as "episodes" (chat messages, unstructured text, or JSON business data). An LLM extracts entities and relations, producing a three-tier graph described in the arXiv paper (2501.13956): (1) episode subgraph G_e holding raw inputs for provenance — every derived fact traces back to its source episode; (2) semantic entity subgraph G_s where entities are nodes and facts are edges stored as triplets (Entity -> Relationship -> Entity) with an embedded "fact string"; (3) community subgraph G_c built by community detection over strongly connected entities, with generated summaries. Bi-temporal model: two timelines — T (event time) and T' (transaction time). Each edge carries four timestamps: t_created and t_expired (when the fact entered/was invalidated in the system, timeline T') plus t_valid and t_invalid (the range the fact held true in the world, timeline T); exposed in the product as created_at/expired_at and valid_at/invalid_at. Edge invalidation: on ingest, an LLM compares new edges against semantically related existing edges; temporally overlapping contradictions cause the old edge to be invalidated (new information is prioritized), but invalidated edges are retained, not deleted — enabling point-in-time queries. Storage backends for OSS Graphiti: Neo4j, FalkorDB, Amazon Neptune (Kuzu deprecated); LLM providers: OpenAI (default, structured output required), Anthropic, Gemini, Groq, Azure OpenAI. READ PATH: hybrid retrieval combining three methods — cosine similarity over embeddings, Okapi BM25 full-text (Lucene), and breadth-first graph traversal within n hops — followed by rerankers: Reciprocal Rank Fusion, Maximal Marginal Relevance, an episode-mentions reranker, a node-distance reranker, and cross-encoder LLM scoring. Zep Cloud exposes a low-level graph.search API and a high-level thread.get_user_context that returns a pre-assembled "Context Block": a user summary plus the most relevant fact strings, each annotated with the dates the fact became valid/invalid. Because retrieval is search over pre-extracted facts (no LLM in the read loop), Zep claims sub-200ms p95 retrieval (homepage: 148ms at 10K graphs to 168ms at 100M graphs — vendor-published, unverified).
token_strategy: Zep substitutes compact, temporally-annotated fact strings and entity/user summaries for raw conversation transcripts. Extraction cost is paid once at ingest (LLM calls); at read time the agent receives a Context Block of "token-efficient context (facts, summaries, and Observations)" rather than message history. Claimed numbers (self-reported, LongMemEval eval in their blog/paper): Zep's retrieved context averaged ~1.6k tokens versus ~115k tokens for the full-context baseline — "less than 2% of the baseline tokens" — while improving accuracy up to 18.5% and cutting median response latency from 28.9s to 2.58s with gpt-4o (~90% reduction, mostly from the smaller prompt). The homepage separately claims 5,760-token context size in a competitive comparison. Billing reinforces the write-heavy design: customers are charged for episode ingestion/processing, not for storage or reads.

benchmarks.claim: Zep 94.8% vs MemGPT's published 93.4% (gpt-4-turbo); Zep's own re-test showed plain gpt-4o with full conversation context scores 98.0%
benchmarks.caveats: Self-reported; arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed. Zep could not replicate MemGPT's original setup and used full-conversation context instead of MemGPT's recursive summarization, so the head-to-head is not apples-to-apples. DMR is small (500 questions) and effectively saturated — Zep itself concedes 'recent advances in LLM capabilities have revealed the DMR benchmark's limitations.' No independent replication found.

benchmarks.claim: Up to 18.5% aggregate accuracy improvement over full-context baseline with individual question types gaining >100% (e.g., single-session-preference with gpt-4o: 20.0% -> 56.7%); temporal reasoning 45.1% -> 62.4% (gpt-4o); 90% latency reduction (median 2.58s vs 28.9s); ~1.6k vs ~115k prompt tokens
benchmarks.caveats: Self-reported; baseline is full-context stuffing, not competing memory systems, so this measures 'better than dumping the transcript,' not superiority over Mem0/Letta. Latency gain largely reflects the smaller prompt. Not independently verified.

benchmarks.claim: Zep's re-run: 75.14% +/- 0.17 J-score vs Mem0's best (graph) config ~68%, and Zep p95 search latency 0.632s vs Mem0 Graph 0.657s; Zep also notes Mem0's own paper shows a full-context baseline (~73%) beating Mem0 (~68%)
benchmarks.caveats: Actively disputed in both directions. Mem0's CTO (github.com/getzep/zep-papers/issues/5) alleges Zep's original 84% figure counted excluded adversarial questions in the numerator only and used non-standard prompts, and that a corrected Zep scores 58.44% +/- 0.20; Zep counter-alleges Mem0 misconfigured Zep (wrong user model, timestamps appended to messages instead of the dedicated field, sequential rather than parallel searches inflating latency) and revised its own figure to 75.14%. Zep further argues LoCoMo itself is flawed: conversations of only ~16k-26k tokens fit in modern context windows, no knowledge-update tests, missing/incorrect ground truth. Unresolved; treat all LoCoMo numbers from both vendors as advocacy.

benchmarks.claim: Sub-200ms p95 retrieval at scale: 148ms at 10K graphs, 152ms at 100K, 156ms at 1M, 168ms at 100M graphs; 1.4M+ active context graphs
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor marketing figures; no methodology published, no independent verification.

benchmarks.claim: Sub-second query latency vs 'seconds to tens of seconds' for GraphRAG-style summarization approaches
benchmarks.caveats: Directional vendor claim in the README comparison table; no published test harness.

pricing: Credit-based, charged on ingestion (not storage or reads). Unit: an Episode (any single object sent — chat message, JSON payload, text block); 1 credit per 350 bytes (or part thereof); webhook invocations 1/8 credit. Tiers (help.getzep.com/pricing via getzep.com, Aug 2026): Free — 10,000 credits/mo, 2 projects, no rollover; Flex — $125/mo ($1,250/yr) with 50,000 credits, 600 RPM, 5 projects, auto top-up $25 per 10K credits, 30-day rollover; Flex Plus — $375/mo ($3,750/yr) with 200,000 credits, 1,000 RPM, 10 projects, observations/custom extraction/webhooks/analytics, 60-day rollover; Zep for Emerging Companies — $13,000/yr (startups with $1M-$10M raised) adding SOC 2 Type II report access, HIPAA BAA, guaranteed rate limits; Enterprise — custom credits/SLA/deployment. Open-source Graphiti is free (Apache 2.0) but you operate your own graph DB and pay your own LLM extraction costs. Funding (per Tracxn/Crunchbase profiles): YC Winter 2024 batch; ~$500K seed reported (Mar/Apr 2024), backers include Y Combinator, Engineering Capital, Step Function; no publicly announced Series A found as of Aug 2026 — funding databases may lag, but this is notably thinner than competitors' publicized raises.
weaknesses: Every headline benchmark number (DMR 94.8%, LongMemEval +18.5%, LoCoMo 75.14%) is self-reported in vendor blog posts or a non-peer-reviewed arXiv preprint; I found no independent third-party replication of any of them.

The LoCoMo dispute cuts both ways: Mem0's public re-evaluation (getzep/zep-papers issue #5) claims Zep's corrected score is 58.44% +/- 0.20, not 84%, alleging an adversarial-question counting error and non-standard prompts; Zep revised to 75.14% and alleges Mem0 misconfigured Zep. Neither side's numbers can be taken at face value.

The DMR win over MemGPT (94.8% vs 93.4%) used a different evaluation protocol than the original MemGPT paper (full-conversation context instead of recursive summarization), and Zep's own data shows vanilla gpt-4o at 98.0% — i.e., the benchmark is saturated and the margin is not meaningful.

Zep Community Edition (the self-hostable Zep server) was deprecated in April 2025 (blog.getzep.com/announcing-a-new-direction-for-zeps-open-source-strategy/); the full Zep product is now cloud-only, creating lock-in — self-hosters get only the lower-level Graphiti library and must run and operate Neo4j/FalkorDB/Neptune themselves.

Write-path cost and latency: every episode requires LLM extraction and contradiction-checking calls, so ingestion is slow and expensive relative to embedding-only systems, and extraction quality degrades with smaller models (Graphiti docs require structured-output-capable LLMs and warn of failures with small models). Ingestion-based credit billing (1 credit/350 bytes) can be hard to forecast for chat-heavy workloads.

Correctness of the graph depends on LLM extraction and LLM-driven edge invalidation — a longstanding HN criticism of LLM-built knowledge graphs is that construction quality is the unsolved problem; errors compound silently in the graph.
Homepage scale and latency claims (1.4M active graphs, sub-200ms p95 at 100M graphs, named customers like Samsung and Zscaler) are unverifiable from public sources.

Publicly documented funding (~$500K seed per Tracxn) is far below rivals (Mem0's publicized raises), raising vendor-viability questions for an enterprise-critical dependency; databases may be lagging but no Series A announcement was findable.
Open-source maintenance friction reported by users, e.g. the official zepai/graphiti Docker image lagging at v0.10 while the library was at v0.22 (getzep/graphiti issue #1030).

summary: Agentic/self-editing memory is the segment of the AI memory-layer market where the LLM itself decides what to remember, edit, and forget via tool calls, rather than a pipeline embedding-and-retrieving passively. As of August 2026 there are four distinct positions: Letta (the MemGPT lineage) is the most architecturally opinionated, having evolved from in-context "memory blocks" plus background sleep-time agents into MemFS, a git-backed memory filesystem with background "dreaming" subagents; LangMem is LangChain's open-source SDK offering semantic/episodic/procedural memory primitives over LangGraph's BaseStore with hot-path tools and background extraction; Anthropic ships a deliberately minimal client-side file-based memory tool (view/create/str_replace/insert/delete/rename under /memories) that pairs with context editing and compaction; OpenAI keeps memory a consumer ChatGPT feature (saved memories plus system-prompt-injected profile aggregates) with no API-level memory primitive, and is sunsetting the Assistants API on August 26, 2026, pushing state management onto developers via the Responses API. The notable convergence is that both Anthropic and Letta have landed on plain files edited by the agent — not vector stores — as the core memory substrate, with retrieval-style embedding search demoted to an optional add-on.
architecture: LETTA (classic MemGPT model, still the conceptual base): Write path — the agent self-edits via tool calls. Core memory is a set of "memory blocks": labeled persistent strings (label, value, size limit in chars/tokens, optional description, unique block_id) stored in a database; edited via core_memory_append/core_memory_replace (or custom tools like rethink_memory that rewrite a whole block). Archival memory is an external embedding-based store written via archival_memory_insert. Recall memory is the full message history, persisted automatically. Blocks can be shared across agents (same block_id attached to multiple agents) or read-only. Read path — Letta "compiles" the context window from DB state each turn (block values rendered via Jinja templating, always in-context); archival_memory_search does semantic search; conversation_search queries recall storage. Sleep-time compute variant: the primary agent has NO core-memory-edit tools; a separate sleep-time agent owns them and asynchronously rewrites the primary agent's blocks, turning "raw context" into "learned context" during idle periods. 2026 EVOLUTION (verified on docs.letta.com): the product now centers on MemFS — a git-backed filesystem of Markdown files with YAML frontmatter. system/ directory files (persona, user preferences, project facts, workflow rules) load into the system prompt every turn; reference files outside system/ are discoverable via the memory tree but loaded only on demand; skills live under $MEMORY_DIR/skills. Every memory edit is a git commit (version history, conflict resolution); background "dreaming" subagents run in git worktrees, review recent conversations, consolidate lessons, and update memory without blocking the main agent, triggered after a configured number of user messages or on context compaction. Notably there is NO built-in semantic index — agents use file-search/read tools; semantic search is an optional mod (QMD integration). LANGMEM: Write path — two modes. Hot path: create_manage_memory_tool lets the agent store/update memories mid-conversation. Background ("subconscious"): create_memory_manager / create_memory_store_manager run an LLM over completed conversations to extract facts, then reconcile against existing memories (update, merge, invalidate contradictions — consolidation). Procedural memory is written by create_prompt_optimizer, which rewrites the agent's system prompt from feedback using metaprompt/gradient/prompt_memory algorithms. Data structures: semantic memory as either "profiles" (a single structured document holding current state, overwritten in place) or "collections" (unbounded individual records); episodic memory as collections of successful interactions (explicitly not yet fully supported); all persisted in LangGraph's BaseStore (InMemoryStore for dev, AsyncPostgresStore for prod) under hierarchical namespaces (org → user → app) with metadata. Read path — create_search_memory_tool does semantic search plus metadata filtering and direct key access at runtime; profiles can be injected wholesale into the prompt. ANTHROPIC MEMORY TOOL (memory_20250818, GA on the Messages API, Claude 4+): Write path — Claude emits tool_use requests with commands create, str_replace, insert, delete, rename against paths under a /memories prefix; the client application executes them against storage it fully controls (filesystem, DB, cloud — SDK helpers like BetaLocalFilesystemMemoryTool exist). The API auto-injects a system-prompt protocol: "ALWAYS VIEW YOUR MEMORY DIRECTORY BEFORE DOING ANYTHING ELSE... ASSUME INTERRUPTION: Your context window might be reset at any moment." Read path — view lists the directory (2 levels deep, sizes) or returns file contents with line numbers, with view_range paging for files over ~16,000 chars. No embeddings, no index, no server-side storage: memory is just files the model reads back on demand (just-in-time retrieval). It composes with context editing (client-side clearing of stale tool results) and server-side compaction (memory preserves what must survive summarization). OPENAI: Consumer ChatGPT memory has two mechanisms. (1) Saved memories: the model calls a bio tool writing timestamped entries into a "Model Set Context" section of the system prompt; user-manageable in settings. (2) "Reference chat history": per independent reverse-engineering (Embrace The Red, validated across two accounts), this is NOT full-text retrieval over past chats — the system injects rolling aggregate sections into the system prompt: Assistant Response Preferences (~15 inferred preferences), Notable Past Conversation Topics, Helpful User Insights (12–14 profile facts with confidence tags), Recent Conversation Content (~40 recent chats: timestamps, summaries, user messages only), and User Interaction Metadata. The researcher explicitly tested and found no recognition of specific year-old conversations. API side: no memory primitive exists; the Assistants API (threads/messages, the closest thing to hosted state) is deprecated with an August 26, 2026 sunset, and the replacement Responses API makes developers manage conversation state themselves via "conversations" objects — memory extraction/consolidation is left to third parties.
token_strategy: The shared thesis of this segment is that agent-curated context beats retrieval-time stuffing. LETTA: fixed-size in-context memory blocks with explicit character/token limits act as a RAM budget; everything else pages to external storage and enters context only via explicit search calls (the OS virtual-memory analogy from the MemGPT paper). MemFS refines this into tiered loading: system/ files always in context, reference material loaded only when relevant, "keeping the active context lean while preserving deeper reference material." Sleep-time compute shifts token spend off the interactive path: the arXiv paper (2504.13171) claims ~5x less test-time compute for equivalent accuracy and 2.5x lower average cost per query when pre-computation is amortized across related queries — though on math benchmarks, not memory workloads. LANGMEM: background ("subconscious") extraction keeps the hot path free of memory-management tokens and latency; the docs explicitly frame hot-path memory tools as adding "perceptible latency"; profiles bound the per-turn context contribution to a single document. LangChain publishes no quantitative token-savings numbers. ANTHROPIC: just-in-time retrieval — record learnings to files, read them back on demand instead of preloading; combined with context editing (auto-clearing stale tool results), Anthropic claims 84% token reduction on a 100-turn web-search evaluation while completing workflows that otherwise fail from context exhaustion (internal, unpublished eval). Memory files also let information survive server-side compaction. OPENAI: bounded, fixed injection — memory sections (saved memories + profile aggregates + ~40 conversation summaries) occupy a roughly constant system-prompt budget regardless of account age; no retrieval calls at inference time and no developer-visible token accounting. WHAT IS GENUINELY DIFFERENT VS RETRIEVAL-BASED MEMORY: (1) the write path is model-driven and destructive — the agent rewrites, merges, and deletes (str_replace, rethink_memory, consolidation) rather than append-only ingestion, so memory is a maintained state, not a growing corpus; (2) reads are agentic navigation (list directory, open file, search conversation) rather than top-k similarity, which trades recall guarantees for coherence and editability; (3) Letta's sleep-time/dreaming and LangMem's background managers move memory formation to idle compute, something retrieval pipelines have no equivalent for; (4) both Anthropic and Letta's 2026 designs drop embeddings from the default path entirely — semantic search is optional, files-plus-grep is the default.

benchmarks.claim: Memory tool + context editing improved performance 39% over baseline; context editing alone +29%
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor claim on an internal, unpublished evaluation set; no task details, baselines, or error bars released; not independently verified.

benchmarks.claim: Context editing (with memory) reduced token consumption by 84% and enabled workflows that otherwise fail from context exhaustion
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor claim, internal eval; the 84% figure is primarily attributed to context editing rather than the memory tool alone.

benchmarks.benchmark: Stateful GSM-Symbolic / Stateful AIME / Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic (sleep-time compute paper)
benchmarks.claim: ~5x reduction in test-time compute at equivalent accuracy; up to +13% (GSM-Symbolic) and +18% (AIME) accuracy from scaling sleep-time compute; 2.5x lower average cost per query when amortized across related queries
benchmarks.caveats: Authored by Letta-affiliated researchers (vendor-adjacent) but public and reproducible in principle; benchmarks are adapted math-reasoning tasks, not agent-memory workloads; gains correlate with query predictability; real-world evidence limited to one SWE case study.

benchmarks.benchmark: MemGPT original evaluations (document analysis, multi-session chat)
benchmarks.claim: MemGPT analyzes documents far exceeding the LLM's native context window and sustains consistent multi-session conversational agents via self-editing memory
benchmarks.caveats: 2023 paper; results are largely qualitative at the abstract level; predates both the current Letta platform and MemFS.

benchmarks.claim: LangChain's launch post and docs make no quantitative performance, recall, or token-efficiency claims for LangMem
benchmarks.caveats: Absence verified against the launch blog, docs index, and conceptual guide; the docs discuss extraction precision/recall tradeoffs only qualitatively.

benchmarks.claim: ChatGPT does not full-text search past conversations; only ~40 recent chats (summaries + user messages) plus rolling profile aggregates are injected into the system prompt, contradicting the implication of 'no storage limit' in OpenAI's help copy
benchmarks.caveats: Independent (Embrace The Red / Johann Rehberger), validated across two accounts, but derived from prompt-dumping which can hallucinate — the author flags this himself; OpenAI may have changed internals since; this is the opposite of a vendor claim and is the best independent evidence available.

pricing: Letta (verified at docs.letta.com/letta-code/pricing, Aug 2026): Free tier with limited agents and limited Letta Auto usage (BYO API keys supported); Pro $20/month (Letta Auto weekly+monthly quota, pay-as-you-go overages, up to 20 stateful agents); API/developer plan $20/month base + $0.10 per active agent/month + $0.00015 per second of tool execution + usage-based LLM costs, unlimited agents; Teams Pro $20/seat/month; Enterprise custom (volume pricing, RBAC, SAML/OIDC SSO). LangMem: MIT-licensed open source, free (pip install langmem); a managed service was offered free at launch; production persistence typically rides on LangGraph Platform, priced separately. Anthropic memory tool: no separate charge — GA on the Messages API, standard token pricing applies; storage is client-side so infrastructure cost is the developer's; memory reads/writes consume normal input/output tokens. OpenAI: ChatGPT memory is bundled into consumer plans (feature availability varies by plan/region); there is no API-priced memory product; Assistants API sunsets August 26, 2026 with the Responses API replacement leaving state management (and its cost) to developers. (OpenAI help-center pages returned HTTP 403 to direct fetches; plan details here come from search-result summaries of those pages and should be re-verified in a browser.)
weaknesses: Letta: the 2026 pivot from memory blocks to MemFS/Letta Code means significant architecture and docs churn — the well-known memory-block model is now described under legacy/blog material while current docs center on MemFS, creating migration burden and making third-party writeups (and benchmarks) stale.

Letta: sleep-time compute's quantitative evidence is from adapted math benchmarks (GSM-Symbolic, AIME), not long-horizon memory tasks; the paper itself notes gains depend on query predictability; and background inference is extra token spend the marketing does not price out.
Letta: MemFS has no built-in semantic search — default retrieval is file navigation and grep; semantic search requires an optional mod, so recall on large memory stores is unproven.

LangMem: episodic memory is explicitly incomplete ('LangMem doesn't yet support opinionated utilities for episodic memory' per LangChain's own launch post); no published benchmarks of any kind; adoption is modest (~1.6k GitHub stars); the stateful layer ties you to LangGraph's BaseStore/Platform.

LangMem: its own docs concede the core quality tradeoff is unsolved — over-extraction degrades search precision, under-extraction hurts recall — and consolidation quality depends entirely on the extraction LLM with no evaluation harness provided.

Anthropic memory tool: everything is the developer's problem — storage backend, path-traversal security (the docs warn /memories/../../secrets.env style attacks must be blocked), file-size caps, and memory expiration; there is no search, no index, and no consolidation service, so memory quality depends wholly on the model's file hygiene.
Anthropic: the headline numbers (39% improvement, 84% token reduction) are from internal, unpublished evaluations with no task detail — vendor claims, not independently verified.

OpenAI: memory is consumer-only and opaque — no API primitive, and the Assistants API sunset (Aug 26, 2026) removes the only hosted-state option; independent analysis shows chat-history 'memory' is rolling profile aggregates over ~40 recent chats, not searchable history, contradicting the marketing framing; documented prompt-injection paths into memory (bio tool invocation, conversation-summary injection) and observed hallucinated memories are real security/reliability concerns.

Cross-cutting: no common benchmark lets these four be compared head-to-head (LoCoMo-style suites cover retrieval systems better than self-editing ones), so every performance claim in this segment is currently vendor-scoped.
