summary: The AI agent memory-layer market has hardened into a funded, benchmarked infrastructure category as of August 2026. Supermemory (founded by ex-Cloudflare DevRel Dhravya Shah, $2.6M seed led by Susa Ventures/Browder Capital/SF1.vc with angels including Jeff Dean and Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht) positions itself as a "memory API" with sub-300ms retrieval claims, an MIT-licensed 28.8k-star repo, and its own open-source benchmark harness (MemoryBench). Around it sit fact-extraction players (Mem0, $24M Series A, 186M API calls in Q3 2025, exclusive memory provider for AWS Agent SDK), graph-native players (Zep/Graphiti, Cognee $7.5M seed, Berlin), agent-OS approaches (Letta/MemGPT, $10M Felicis seed), file/markdown-native approaches (Dria's mem-agent 4B model, Supermemory's SMFS), a human-memory-inspired open-source entrant (Vectorize's Hindsight, claiming 91.4% on LongMemEval), a visual-memory specialist (Memories.ai, $16M total, NVIDIA/Qualcomm/Samsung partnerships, pivoting toward wearables/robotics), and a parametric-memory outlier (Engram, $98M at $600M valuation, compressing org knowledge into learned model memory rather than retrieval). The market is converging on three retrieval-side architectures — LLM fact extraction, temporal knowledge graphs, and agent-traversable file systems — while every vendor publishes benchmarks on which it ranks first, so almost no performance claim in this space is independently verified.
architecture: SUPERMEMORY (primary subject). Write path (vendor-described, hosted API closed-source): ingestion via POST /v3/documents plus connectors (Google Drive, Gmail, Notion, OneDrive, GitHub, S3) with "Extractors" for PDFs, web pages, images (OCR), audio/video (transcription), and code. A "Memory Engine" extracts facts, tracks updates, resolves contradictions, and applies automatic forgetting; content is deduplicated at ingest (billing is per unique "SM token"). Storage is a "custom vector graph engine with ontology-aware edges" — i.e., vector index plus graph relationships, not a plain vector DB — plus per-user dynamic profiles (static facts + evolving context). Read path: POST /v3/search with hybrid retrieval (vector + keyword/full-text) plus graph traversal and profile injection; vendor claims sub-300ms end-to-end retrieval and ~50ms user-profile reads. Distribution: TS/Python SDKs, REST API, MCP server, self-hostable local binary (client stack MIT-licensed; hosted infrastructure not open-sourced). Their newer SMFS is a FUSE-based agent filesystem: semantic search finds an anchor file path, then the agent reads/greps/traverses neighboring files — a hybrid of RAG and agentic file exploration, with an auto-updating /profile.md. COMPARATIVE ARCHITECTURES verified this session: Mem0 = LLM-powered fact extraction into a memory store shared across apps ("memory passport"); Zep = temporal knowledge graph construction (Graphiti); Cognee = graph-native ECL (Extract-Cognify-Load) pipeline turning raw data into queryable knowledge graphs, open source (~12k stars) with cloud and a Rust edge engine in development; Hindsight (Vectorize, MIT) = four memory networks separating facts/experiences/observations/opinions with confidence-scored beliefs and three operations (Retain, Recall, Reflect), entity/time-anchored for temporal reasoning; mem-agent (Dria) = a 4B Qwen3 fine-tune trained with online RL to operate an Obsidian-like markdown memory (retrieval/update/clarification), used as an MCP sidecar to a larger model; LlamaIndex = composable memory blocks (StaticMemoryBlock, FactExtractionMemoryBlock, VectorMemoryBlock) fed by a FIFO short-term queue that flushes to long-term blocks with priority-based token budgeting; Pinecone Assistant = managed doc-grounded RAG/chat with citations, but its docs show no persistent cross-session memory feature — Pinecone remains the storage substrate under other memory systems rather than a memory product; Engram = the anti-retrieval bet, pre-training ("study once") company context into compact reusable model memory instead of querying an index per request.
token_strategy: Every player pitches token reduction as the core economic argument, with mostly vendor-supplied numbers. Supermemory claims "95% Recall@15 with a 99.4% context reduction" on LongMemEval/LoCoMo/ConvoMem (their GitHub README; measured on their own MemoryBench harness) — i.e., send a few retrieved memories instead of full history. Their SMFS post claims 53.8% fewer tokens and 55% lower cost ($2,103 → $946 across an evaluation; $20.95 → $4.71 on one query class) versus a baseline agentic-search setup, with accuracy rising from 69% to 81% at 10,000 files — but this is measured on xAFS, a benchmark Supermemory created for the launch. MemoryBench itself makes contextTokens a first-class metric: its MemScore is an accuracy%/latencyMs/contextTokens triple, explicitly refusing to collapse cost into a single score. LlamaIndex reduces tokens structurally via priority-ranked memory blocks under a token limit. mem-agent offloads memory management to a cheap 4B local model so the frontier model never sees raw memory files. Engram is the most aggressive claim: compressing organizational knowledge into learned model memory yields "up to 100x fewer tokens than frontier models" (vendor claim, no public benchmark found). None of these token-reduction figures have independent third-party replication that I could locate.

benchmarks.benchmark: MemoryBench (Supermemory's own harness: LoCoMo + LongMemEval + ConvoMem)
benchmarks.claim: Supermemory ranks #1 across all three datasets; README headline is 95% Recall@15 with 99.4% context reduction and ~50ms user-profile reads. Harness runs a checkpointed INGEST→SEARCH→ANSWER→EVALUATE→REPORT pipeline, reports MemScore (accuracy%/latencyMs/contextTokens), is judge-agnostic (GPT-4o/Claude/Gemini), and ships pluggable providers: Supermemory (chunk-based semantic search), Mem0 (LLM fact extraction), Zep (knowledge graph).
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor-authored benchmark on which the vendor ranks first. Only two competitors integrated (Mem0, Zep); no evidence competitors' configurations were tuned. Open-source and reproducible in principle, but I found no independent third-party reproduction. Underlying datasets (LoCoMo especially) have known annotation-quality criticisms.

benchmarks.claim: Hindsight (Vectorize) claims 89.0% with gpt-oss-120B and 91.4% with Gemini-3 — described in third-party roundups as the first memory system past 90% — and +44.6 points over full-context baselines, beating Zep and Supermemory with comparable or smaller models.
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor blog; self-run evaluation. Open-source (MIT) so replicable, but no independent verification found. Note different vendors claim leadership on the same benchmark (Supermemory also claims #1 on LongMemEval via MemoryBench), which is only possible because each runs its own harness, judge, and answering model.

benchmarks.claim: SMFS: 81% accuracy at 10,000 files vs 69% baseline; 55% cost reduction ($2,103→$946); 53.8% fewer tokens; per-query cost $20.95→$4.71. Benchmark uses up to 10k coherent files of 10k+ tokens with multi-hop and temporal questions; runs published at smfs.ai/research/runs.
benchmarks.caveats: Benchmark was purpose-built by the vendor for this product launch; baseline choice controls the headline number. Public run logs improve auditability but no third party has validated the setup.

benchmarks.claim: mem-agent (4B, Qwen3-4B-Thinking fine-tune, online RL) scores 0.75 vs 0.39 for the base model; second overall, beating all open and closed models except Qwen3-235B-thinking.
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor-created benchmark measuring markdown-memory operations, not end-to-end conversational QA; not comparable to LongMemEval/LoCoMo numbers.

benchmarks.claim: Sub-300ms memory retrieval; ~50ms user-profile reads.
benchmarks.caveats: Marketing-page and README claims; no percentile definition (p50 vs p95), no test conditions, no independent measurement found. MemoryBench does record per-provider latency, but those runs are vendor-executed.

benchmarks.claim: 41k+ GitHub stars, 13M+ Python downloads, 80k+ cloud developers, API calls growing 35M (Q1 2025) → 186M (Q3 2025, ~30% MoM); exclusive memory provider for AWS Agent SDK.
benchmarks.caveats: Company-supplied figures reported by TechCrunch, not audited; included as the best available independent-press reporting of usage in this market.

pricing: Supermemory (verified from supermemory.ai/pricing): subscription + usage hybrid. Free $0 (~$5/mo usage included, MCP + Hermes plugin); Pro $19/mo (~$20 usage, 2 teammates, Drive/Notion/OneDrive connectors); Max $100/mo (~$130 usage, Gmail/Granola connectors); Scale $399/mo (~$600 usage, 10 teammates, SOC 2 + HIPAA BAA, self-hosted option); Enterprise custom (air-gapped self-hosting, FDE, SLA). Usage meters: Memory $0.005/1K "SM tokens" plain text ($0.010 rich), SuperRAG $0.001/1K ($0.002 rich), Search $0.005/1K queries, Operations $0.10/1K ops; SM tokens are deduplicated so re-ingested content is free. Comparables from this research: Pinecone introduced a $50/mo platform minimum (Sept 2025, per third-party roundups — not verified on Pinecone's own pricing page); Mem0, Zep, Letta, Cognee cloud pricing not examined this session. Engram pricing not public.
weaknesses: Benchmark circularity is endemic: Supermemory ranks #1 on its own MemoryBench, Hindsight claims SOTA on its own LongMemEval runs, Dria leads its own md-memory-bench, and SMFS's 55%-cheaper claim rests on xAFS, a benchmark Supermemory invented for the launch. No independent lab or academic replication of any leading vendor's numbers was found.

Supermemory funding data is noisy: TechCrunch (primary, Oct 6 2025) reports a $2.6M seed; an aggregator-derived summary claimed '$26M seed / $29M total,' which appears to be a decimal misparse of the same round and could not be verified anywhere — treat $2.6M as the real figure. That is a very small war chest against Mem0 ($24M), Cognee ($7.5M), and Engram ($98M).

Supermemory's hosted engine — the thing the latency and accuracy claims are about — is closed-source; the 28.8k-star repo is the app/SDK/local stack, so the star count overstates verifiable openness of the core product.
Latency claims across the market (sub-300ms, ~50ms profiles) lack percentile definitions, load conditions, and third-party measurement.
MemoryBench compares only three providers (Supermemory, Mem0, Zep); Letta, Cognee, Hindsight, and LangMem are absent, and there is no evidence competitor configurations were tuned by their own teams.

Pinecone's Assistant product shows no persistent cross-session memory in its docs — incumbent RAG platforms are further behind on memory than marketing suggests, with LlamaIndex's memory blocks (in-framework, developer-managed) the more substantive incumbent response.

Unsolved problems across all players: temporal reasoning and knowledge updates (every benchmark's weakest category), principled forgetting/consolidation vs. unbounded growth, write-time LLM-extraction cost vs read-time latency tradeoffs, cross-app memory portability ('memory passport' remains aspirational), multi-user/org-level memory permissions, and privacy of accumulating personal profiles.

Platform risk: TechCrunch notes OpenAI and other labs are building first-party memory as a moat; if frontier models ship good native memory (or ultra-long context plus caching gets cheap), the standalone retrieval-memory layer gets squeezed — Engram's parametric approach is a bet that this squeeze happens.
Market-sizing signals are round-based, not revenue-based: no vendor in this space discloses revenue; hiring and API-call growth are the only public demand proxies.

summary: The storage/search infra market for an agent-memory API built on Postgres + pgvector is in a strong position as of August 2026: pgvector 0.8.x added iterative index scans (strict_order/relaxed_order) that largely fix the filtered-search over/under-fetch problem, plus halfvec (fp16, 4,000-dim HNSW cap vs 2,000 for float32) and binary quantization with rescoring. Timescale's pgvectorscale extension (StreamingDiskANN + statistical binary quantization, label-based filtered search per Microsoft's Filtered DiskANN) extends single-node Postgres to ~50M vectors with vendor-claimed 28x lower p95 latency and 16x higher QPS than Pinecone s1 at 99% recall on 50M 768-dim Cohere embeddings — though it is not installable on RDS/Aurora, only self-hosted or Timescale/Tiger Cloud. Dedicated vector DBs now compete mostly on cost architecture rather than raw ANN quality: Pinecone serverless ($0.33/GB-mo storage, ~$16-24/M read units, $50/mo minimum on Standard), turbopuffer (object-storage-first, $16/mo Launch minimum, query pricing cut to $1/PB base in Feb 2026, warm p50 ~14ms vs cold ~874ms on 1M docs), Qdrant/Weaviate/Zilliz (provisioned-resource pricing), and LanceDB (embedded, Lance columnar format, usage-based cloud in beta). For hybrid search, native tsvector still lacks BM25 (no IDF, no length normalization), and ParadeDB's pg_search (Tantivy-based, AGPLv3) plus Timescale's new pg_textsearch are the credible in-Postgres BM25 options. The realistic single-node pgvector ceiling with 1,536-dim embeddings is roughly 5-10M vectors on ordinary instances and ~50-100M with pgvectorscale/halfvec/large RAM; past that, index build times (hours), HNSW's no-space-reclamation on deletes, and >600GB raw storage at 100M vectors force partitioning, disk-native indexes (DiskANN/ScaNN), or a dedicated engine.
architecture: WRITE PATH options observed in the market: (1) pgvector single node — embeddings stored in a vector/halfvec column (4 bytes/dim + 8, or 2 bytes/dim + 8); HNSW index built in maintenance_work_mem (Neon docs: set to working-set size but <=50-60% of RAM; parallel build via max_parallel_maintenance_workers; a 7CU/28GB Neon compute uses maintenance_work_mem='10GB' + 7 workers), defaults m=16, ef_construction=64; HNSW does NOT reclaim space on delete, so high-churn memory workloads accumulate index bloat and need REINDEX CONCURRENTLY. IVFFlat builds ~6x faster (dbi-services: 5s vs 29s at 25K x 3,072-dim) but needs representative data upfront. (2) pgvectorscale — Rust extension adding a StreamingDiskANN graph laid out for SSD residency with statistical binary quantization; dbi-services measured a 21MB DiskANN index vs 193MB HNSW on the same 25K x 3,072-dim data (~9x smaller); labels for filtered search must be smallint arrays queried with &&; no parallel build with labels, no UNLOGGED tables. (3) turbopuffer — WAL written directly to object storage (S3) with group commits, 1 WAL entry/sec/namespace, ~10K vectors/sec throughput but p50 write latency ~165ms; indexes built async from the WAL. (4) Pinecone serverless — writes billed as write units, storage decoupled at $0.33/GB-mo. READ PATH: pgvector HNSW query walks the graph with hnsw.ef_search (default 40); since 0.8.0, iterative index scans keep pulling candidates until the WHERE clause is satisfied (strict_order = exact distance order; relaxed_order = better recall; max_scan_tuples default 20,000 bounds tail latency) — this is the critical feature for tenant-scoped memory queries; binary_quantize + Hamming coarse pass then cosine rescore is the two-phase pattern for big tables. turbopuffer routes queries to a node that caches the namespace on NVMe/memory (cold 1M-doc query p50 874ms with 3-4 object-storage roundtrips; warm p50 14ms). AlloyDB replaces HNSW with ScaNN (tree-quantization, Google Research), claiming 4x smaller memory footprint and graceful behavior when the index exceeds RAM (431ms vs >4s for HNSW). Hybrid search: ParadeDB pg_search maintains a Tantivy inverted index (BM25 scoring, positions, highlighting) inside Postgres blocks, combined with pgvector via SQL-level fusion (e.g., RRF); native tsvector/ts_rank scores only term frequency + length weighting with no corpus-level IDF.
token_strategy: Not directly applicable — this is storage infra, not an answer-generation layer, and no vendor in this space publishes token-reduction claims. The relevant mechanism for a memory API: retrieval precision is what bounds tokens sent to the model, so infra choices matter indirectly. (a) Filtered ANN quality (pgvector iterative scans, pgvectorscale label filters, ScaNN filtering) determines whether tenant/agent-scoped top-k actually returns the k most relevant memories instead of post-filter dropouts that force larger k. (b) In-Postgres BM25 (pg_search/pg_textsearch) enables hybrid dense+lexical retrieval with RRF in one SQL query, which raises precision@k so fewer, better memories go into context. (c) Postgres co-location lets metadata predicates (recency, memory type, importance) run in the same plan, avoiding over-fetch-then-rerank pipelines. Any concrete 'X% fewer tokens' number would come from the memory layer above this infra, not the infra itself.
pricing: Pinecone serverless (pinecone.io/pricing, fetched Aug 2026): Starter free; Builder $20/mo flat; Standard $50/mo minimum; Enterprise $500/mo minimum. Storage $0.33/GB/mo; read units $16-18/M (Standard) or $24-27/M (Enterprise), write units $4-4.50/M (Standard); backups $0.10/GB/mo; HIPAA add-on $190/mo. turbopuffer: Launch $16/mo minimum (cut from $64 in June 2026), Scale $256/mo, Enterprise >=$4,096/mo with 35% usage premium; query base rate cut from $5/PB to $1/PB scanned (Feb 2026) with up to 96% marginal discounts; per-GB storage/write rates live in a JS calculator I could not extract — third-party sources cite ~$0.07/GB-mo storage and ~$0.02/GB effective for cold object storage, UNVERIFIED against the vendor page. Weaviate Cloud: Free tier (100K objects); Flex from $45/mo at $0.00465 per million stored dimensions; Premium from $400/mo at $0.002718-0.003875 per million dimensions; storage $0.12-0.15/GiB. Zilliz Cloud (managed Milvus, via search results): serverless $4 per million vCUs; dedicated ~$0.096/CU-hour compute + $0.02/GB/mo storage. Qdrant Cloud: provisioned resource pricing (RAM/CPU/disk), no per-vector metering; third-party estimates ~$114/mo for 1M x 1536-dim with quantization, ~$0.078/GB-hour — estimates, not vendor-verified. LanceDB: OSS Apache 2.0 free; Cloud is usage-based serverless in public beta ($100 free credits), enterprise via annual commit — no public rate card found. Managed Postgres: Neon/Supabase charge normal compute+storage with pgvector free (Supabase free tier works for small vector sets); RDS/Aurora/Cloud SQL/AlloyDB charge standard instance pricing — Aurora Optimized Reads (NVMe-cache instances) claims 75-80% lower cost-per-query for HNSW workloads exceeding RAM. Reference self-hosted anchor (Timescale, June 2024): 50M x 768-dim on EC2 ~$835/mo vs Pinecone s1 $3,241/mo / p2 $3,889/mo.

benchmarks.claim: Postgres + pgvector + pgvectorscale: 28x lower p95 latency and 16x higher QPS than Pinecone s1 at 99% recall; 1.4x lower p95 / 1.5x higher QPS than p2 at 90% recall; ~75% cheaper self-hosted ($835/mo EC2 vs $3,241-3,889/mo)
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor (Timescale/Tiger Data) benchmark from June 2024 against Pinecone's pre-2024 pod-based s1/p2 indexes, not current serverless; Pinecone doesn't expose recall tuning, so the 99%-recall comparison is inherently asymmetric; not independently reproduced

benchmarks.benchmark: Qdrant single-node benchmarks (dbpedia-openai-1M-1536d, deep-image-10M-96d, gist-960-1M, glove-100)
benchmarks.claim: Qdrant achieves highest RPS and lowest latency in almost all scenarios vs Weaviate, Milvus, Elasticsearch, Redis; Elasticsearch ~10x slower indexing at 10M+ vectors
benchmarks.caveats: Self-run vendor benchmark, last updated Jan/Jun 2024 (filtered-search section Feb 2023 — stale); pgvector not included; all engines Docker-constrained to 25GB RAM; open-sourced harness but results not third-party verified

benchmarks.claim: Up to 4x lower latency even on small datasets; 10x better when index exceeds memory (431ms vs >4s); 4x smaller memory footprint; billion-vector index builds at claimed 60x lower cost
benchmarks.caveats: Google vendor claims (blog + whitepaper); predates pgvector 0.8.x iterative scans; ScaNN index is AlloyDB-proprietary, so adopting it is GCP lock-in

benchmarks.benchmark: Aurora Optimized Reads with pgvector HNSW
benchmarks.claim: Up to 9x average query throughput and 75-80% lower cost per query vs standard Aurora instances when the vector working set exceeds RAM (NVMe tiered caching)
benchmarks.caveats: AWS vendor claim; benefit only materializes once indexes spill past memory; Aurora supports pgvector 0.8.0 but NOT pgvectorscale (confirmed unavailable on RDS/Aurora per AWS re:Post)

benchmarks.benchmark: dbi-services pgvector index comparison, 25K Wikipedia articles x 3,072-dim (text-embedding-3-large)
benchmarks.claim: HNSW build 29s/193MB index; IVFFlat 5s/193MB; pgvectorscale DiskANN 49s/21MB (~9x smaller); binary quantization gives ~97% storage reduction with Hamming-then-rescore two-phase search
benchmarks.caveats: Independent consultancy (not a vector-DB vendor) and recent (March 2026), but tiny dataset (25K rows) chosen for pedagogy; absolute numbers don't extrapolate to 10M+ scale

benchmarks.benchmark: ParadeDB pg_search vs native Postgres FTS (tsvector), 1M rows
benchmarks.claim: pg_search indexes ~50s faster than tsvector at 1M rows and ranks results ~20x faster; tsvector's ts_rank lacks IDF and document-length normalization entirely, so it is not BM25-quality ranking regardless of speed
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor benchmark; ParadeDB also claims parity with a dedicated Elasticsearch instance on indexing/search time but publishes fewer specifics; pg_search is AGPLv3 (enterprise license for commercial embedding); not available on RDS — Neon does offer it

benchmarks.claim: Cold query (from object storage, 3-4 S3 roundtrips) p50 ~874ms; NVMe/memory-warm p50 ~14ms; writes ~10K vectors/sec but p50 write latency 165ms (1 WAL commit/sec/namespace)
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor-published numbers from their own architecture page; the cold/warm gap means latency SLOs depend entirely on cache residency — fine for per-agent memory namespaces queried in sessions, risky for uniformly random access across many cold tenants

benchmarks.claim: Production pgvector comfortable to ~10M vectors/node; pgvectorscale extends to ~50M with p95 <50ms (471 QPS at 99% recall on 50M reported)
benchmarks.caveats: Secondary-source roundup repeating vendor numbers; useful as consensus rule-of-thumb, not as independent measurement

weaknesses: Filtered search remains pgvector's weakest area even after 0.8.x: iterative scans fix correctness (no more silently empty results) but pay for it in CPU, memory, and tail latency on highly selective filters — exactly the tenant_id + agent_id + memory_type predicates a multi-tenant memory API runs on every query; partitioning or pgvectorscale label filters (smallint-array labels only, && operator, no parallel build) are the workarounds.

HNSW indexes do not reclaim space on row deletion — a high-churn memory layer (consolidation, decay, versioned rewrites) will bloat the index and needs periodic REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, which is expensive at tens of GB.

pgvectorscale, the strongest pgvector scaling story, cannot be installed on RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, or Supabase — it effectively ties you to self-hosted Postgres or Timescale/Tiger Cloud, which undercuts the 'just use managed Postgres' pitch.

Nearly every headline performance number in this market is a vendor self-benchmark (Timescale vs Pinecone, Qdrant vs everyone, Google ScaNN vs HNSW, ParadeDB vs tsvector/Elasticsearch); the only genuinely independent recent measurement found (dbi-services, March 2026) uses a 25K-row dataset too small to test scale claims. No neutral 2025-2026 benchmark of pgvector 0.8.x iterative scans vs dedicated engines on filtered workloads was found.

Timescale's Pinecone comparison is dated June 2024 and targeted Pinecone's old pod-based s1/p2 tiers; Pinecone serverless has since restructured pricing entirely, so the 28x/16x/75% numbers should not be quoted against 2026 Pinecone serverless.

turbopuffer's granular pricing (per-GB storage and write rates) is only exposed via a JavaScript calculator that could not be scraped; the ~$0.07/GB-mo and ~$2/GB-write figures circulating are third-party and unverified. Its 1-write-commit/sec/namespace and ~874ms cold-query latency are real constraints for low-latency memory reads over many cold namespaces.

Hard vector-count ceilings quoted everywhere (~10M/node pgvector, ~50M with pgvectorscale) are rules of thumb dominated by memory economics, not cliffs: 100M x 1536-dim float32 is >600GB raw before HNSW overhead, index builds take hours, and ef_search >200 can flip the planner to sequential scans — but halfvec, binary quantization, partitioning, and NVMe-cached instances (Aurora Optimized Reads) all move the line, so the true threshold is workload-specific.

In-Postgres BM25 is young: ParadeDB pg_search is AGPLv3 (license risk for a commercial API), unavailable on the major hyperscaler managed Postgres offerings (available on Neon), and its own 'native vector + hybrid search' is still marked coming soon; Timescale's pg_textsearch 1.0 lacks phrase queries (no term positions stored). Native tsvector ranking has no IDF and no length normalization, so it is not a serious BM25 substitute for memory retrieval quality.
LanceDB Cloud pricing is effectively unpublished (usage-based beta, no rate card), making cost comparison impossible from primary sources.

Qdrant's filtered-search benchmark section dates to Feb 2023 — pre-dating pgvector HNSW entirely — and its cloud pricing requires a calculator; per-million-vector figures in circulation are third-party estimates.

summary: Token reduction for agent memory/RAG context, as of August 2026, is pursued at three layers: write-time distillation (LLM fact/triple extraction, salience filtering, hierarchical/recursive summarization, deduplication — the core of commercial memory layers like Mem0, Zep, Letta), read-time compression (extractive/abstractive compressors like RECOMP, token-pruning compressors like LLMLingua-1/2, learned soft-token compression like gisting/ICAE, and progressive/agentic retrieval where the model pages in more context on demand), and serving-side caching (provider cached-token discounts of 75-90% and KV-cache reuse via prefix/radix caching). Published papers support 2-6x task-agnostic compression with near-parity quality, 10-20x in favorable settings (redundant CoT prompts, extractive RAG summarization), and ~90%+ read-time token savings for fact-extraction memory versus full-context replay — but an independent 2026 cost-performance study found long-context models with prompt caching still beat fact-based memory on factual recall (LongMemEval, LoCoMo), so the savings are not free. Vendor benchmark numbers in this market are actively disputed (the Zep-vs-Mem0 LoCoMo fight saw one score revised from 84% to 58.44% and re-rebutted to 75.14%), so single-number vendor claims should be treated as marketing until independently reproduced.
architecture: Canonical memory-layer write path (per Mem0 arXiv:2504.19413 and Zep arXiv:2501.13956): incoming messages go through an LLM extraction pass that emits discrete natural-language facts or subject-predicate-object triples; an update/consolidation phase compares each candidate against existing memories (vector similarity + LLM judgment) and applies ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP operations — this is where deduplication and contradiction resolution happen. Storage is a vector index over fact strings (Mem0 base), optionally a knowledge graph: Zep's Graphiti engine stores a temporally-aware graph with entity nodes, relation edges carrying validity intervals (bi-temporal: event time vs ingestion time), plus entity summaries; Mem0's graph variant (Mem0g) adds entity-relation triples on top of facts. Mem0's 2026 revision moved to single-pass ADD-only extraction (halving extraction latency, preserving historical state changes) with separate entity embedding stores for entity linking. Hierarchical summarization variants (MemGPT arXiv:2310.08560; recursive summarization arXiv:2308.15022; Anthropic's compaction guidance) maintain session summaries that are recursively folded into a running memory, with raw history demoted to searchable recall storage. Read path: query-time retrieval (vector similarity, plus BM25/keyword and entity-match fusion in Mem0's 2026 pipeline; graph traversal + semantic search in Zep) returns a small set of facts/subgraphs/summaries assembled into the prompt — typically 1-2K tokens (Mem0 paper: ~1.8K) to ~7K tokens (Mem0 2026 algorithm) instead of replaying 25-26K+ tokens of raw history. Read-time compressors sit between retriever and LLM: RECOMP (arXiv:2310.04408) trains an extractive compressor (contrastive sentence selection) and an abstractive compressor (distilled from GPT-3.5/4) that shrink retrieved documents to as little as 5-6% of original tokens; LLMLingua-2 (arXiv:2403.12968) is a task-agnostic XLM-RoBERTa-large token classifier (keep/drop per token) trained by data distillation from GPT-4. Progressive/agentic retrieval (MemGPT's OS-style paging between main context and archival storage via self-issued function calls; Anthropic's "just-in-time" pattern of holding lightweight identifiers — file paths, stored queries — and loading content via tools only when needed) replaces bulk pre-retrieval with on-demand reads. Serving side: providers hash stable prompt prefixes and reuse KV caches (Anthropic explicit cache_control breakpoints with prefix-hash lookback over up to 20 block positions; OpenAI automatic caching of prefixes ≥1024 tokens in 128-token increments; Gemini implicit caching by default on 2.5+ models plus explicit cache objects). Self-hosted equivalents: SGLang's RadixAttention keeps KV caches in a radix tree keyed by token-sequence prefix with LRU eviction (arXiv:2312.07104); vLLM's automatic prefix caching hashes fixed-size blocks. Design consequence: memory content injected as a stable, append-only prefix caches well; per-query dynamically compressed or re-ranked context breaks prefix identity and forfeits cache discounts.
token_strategy: Write-time: fact extraction compresses conversation history into discrete facts — Mem0's paper claims >90% token savings (~1.8K tokens per conversation vs 26K full-context) with 91% lower p95 latency; its 2026 algorithm targets <7K tokens per retrieval call vs 25K+ full-context (~3-4x). Caveat these are read-time savings; write-time itself spends LLM calls per message (extraction + update judgment), a cost the headline numbers exclude. Recursive/hierarchical summarization (arXiv:2308.15022, MemGPT, Anthropic compaction) bounds context growth to a constant-size summary; measured gains are consistency/recall improvements rather than published compression ratios. Deduplication is implemented as ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP consolidation (Mem0) or graph entity resolution (Zep); no isolated compression numbers are published for dedup alone. Read-time: LLMLingua-1 reports up to 20x compression on GSM8K CoT prompts with accuracy 78.85%→77.94%; LongLLMLingua reports 4x compression with up to +17.1-21.4% accuracy on NaturalQuestions (compression can help by removing distractors/position bias), 1.4-2.6x latency reduction, and 94% cost reduction on LooGLE; LLMLingua-2 is more honest about the task-agnostic regime — 2-5x compression, 1.6-2.9x end-to-end latency, near-parity on MeetingBank/LongBench/GSM8K/BBH with a small encoder that is 3-6x faster than LLMLingua-1. RECOMP compresses retrieved docs to ~6% of tokens (≈16x) with minimal loss on language modeling and open-domain QA; at 5% tokens it loses only ~3.7 EM vs full documents. Soft/learned compression (context distillation family): gist tokens (arXiv:2304.08467) achieve up to 26x prompt compression and ~40% FLOPs reduction with minimal quality loss, ICAE ~15x — but these require finetuning the serving model, so they are unusable with closed API models where the memory-layer market lives. Structured fact tables vs prose: direct controlled comparisons are scarce; the strongest independent evidence (arXiv:2603.04814) shows flat-typed fact extraction works for stable attributes but loses to long-context prose replay on LongMemEval/LoCoMo recall. Progressive/agentic retrieval avoids paying for unused context by letting the model request more (MemGPT function-call paging: 92.5% deep-memory-retrieval accuracy vs 32.1% for baseline GPT-4; Anthropic recommends hybrid: small always-on memory plus just-in-time tool loads, at the cost of added latency and turn count). Serving-side: cached input tokens cost 0.1x base at Anthropic (write premium 1.25x for 5-min TTL, 2x for 1-hr; 512-4096 token minimum by model), 0.1x at OpenAI (90% discount, automatic ≥1024-token prefixes, cache lifetime ~5-10 min up to 1 hr) and ~0.1x at Gemini (plus explicit-cache storage of $1.00-4.50 per M tokens per hour). This means a stable 100K-token memory prefix re-read each turn costs roughly one-tenth of naive input pricing — arXiv:2603.04814 factors this in and finds long-context + caching becomes cost-competitive with fact-based memory until ~10 interaction turns at 100K context, after which fixed-size memory reads win on cost.

benchmarks.claim: LLMLingua-1 achieves up to 20x compression with accuracy 78.85% -> 77.94% (near-lossless); LLMLingua-2 holds parity up to ~14x on 9-step CoT prompts
benchmarks.caveats: Best-case ratios on highly redundant few-shot CoT prompts; task-agnostic compression of arbitrary retrieved context is 2-5x, not 20x. Microsoft's own project page, but numbers match the peer-reviewed papers.

benchmarks.claim: LongLLMLingua: 4x compression with up to +17.1-21.4% accuracy (compression removes distractors and mitigates lost-in-the-middle), 1.4-2.6x latency reduction, 94% cost reduction on LooGLE
benchmarks.caveats: Accuracy gain is question-aware and depends on retrieval noise being present; requires a small LLaMA-class model for perplexity scoring at inference time.

benchmarks.benchmark: MeetingBank, LongBench, ZeroScrolls, GSM8K, BBH (task-agnostic compression)
benchmarks.claim: LLMLingua-2: 2-5x compression at near-parity quality, 3-6x faster compressor than LLMLingua-1, 1.6-2.9x end-to-end latency reduction, using XLM-RoBERTa-large token classifier
benchmarks.caveats: ACL 2024 Findings, peer-reviewed. Out-of-domain performance holds but compressor was trained only on MeetingBank distillations from GPT-4.

benchmarks.benchmark: NQ / TriviaQA / HotpotQA + WikiText LM (RAG compression)
benchmarks.claim: RECOMP compresses retrieved documents to as low as 6% of tokens (~16x) with minimal performance loss; at 5% tokens loses only ~3.7 EM vs prepending full documents
benchmarks.caveats: Consulted via search results and abstract, not full-text verified. Compressors are trained per task family; abstractive compressor distilled from proprietary LLMs; selective augmentation can return empty context when retrieval is useless.

benchmarks.claim: Gist tokens: up to 26x prompt compression, ~40% FLOPs reduction, 4.2% wall-time speedup with minimal quality loss; ICAE caps around 15x
benchmarks.caveats: Consulted via search summaries. Requires finetuning the target model (attention-mask modification); compressed tokens do not transfer to untuned/closed API models — largely irrelevant to API-based memory products, relevant to self-hosted serving.

benchmarks.claim: Mem0 paper: 26% relative LLM-as-a-Judge improvement over OpenAI memory (66.9% vs 52.9%), >90% token savings (~1.8K vs 26K tokens per conversation), 91% lower p95 latency (1.44s vs 17.12s); graph variant ~2% higher
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor-authored paper (accepted ECAI 2025). LoCoMo itself has documented flaws (speaker misattribution, ambiguous questions). Token savings count read-time only; write-time extraction/update LLM calls are extra.

benchmarks.claim: Zep/Graphiti temporal knowledge graph: 94.8% vs MemGPT 93.4% on DMR; up to +18.5% accuracy on LongMemEval with ~90% latency reduction vs full-context baseline
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor-authored preprint. DMR delta over MemGPT is 1.4 points. Zep's separate 84% LoCoMo claim was challenged by Mem0 (corrected eval: 58.44%, per https://github.com/getzep/zep-papers/issues/5); Zep counter-claims 75.14% and accuses Mem0 of misconfiguration (https://blog.getzep.com/lies-damn-lies-statistics-is-mem0-really-sota-in-agent-memory/). Treat all LoCoMo vendor numbers as contested.

benchmarks.claim: MemGPT self-directed paging (progressive retrieval via function calls) achieves 92.5% accuracy vs 32.1% for fixed-context GPT-4 baseline
benchmarks.caveats: Academic paper (authors later founded Letta, so now vendor-adjacent). Paging adds multi-turn latency and extra LLM calls per retrieval decision; DMR is a small synthetic benchmark.

benchmarks.claim: Fact-based memory becomes cheaper than long-context replay only after ~10 interaction turns at 100K context (with prompt caching modeled); long-context GPT-5-mini achieves HIGHER factual recall than the fact-based memory system on LongMemEval and LoCoMo; memory competitive only on PersonaMemv2 (stable flat-typed attributes)
benchmarks.caveats: Single memory implementation tested; results depend on cache-hit assumptions. This is the clearest independent evidence that write-time hard compression trades away recall quality.

benchmarks.claim: Vendor blog claims LoCoMo 92.5 (from 71.4), LongMemEval 94.4 (from 67.8), BEAM-1M 64.1 at 6,719 mean tokens, under 7K tokens per retrieval vs 25K+ full context, via single-pass ADD-only extraction, dedup + entity linking, and 3-signal retrieval fusion
benchmarks.caveats: Pure vendor marketing, not peer-reviewed, no independent reproduction found; directly conflicts with the independent finding in arXiv:2603.04814 that memory systems trail long-context on these same benchmarks. Unverified.

benchmarks.claim: SGLang RadixAttention (radix-tree KV cache reuse across calls with LRU eviction) delivers up to 5x throughput vs contemporary vLLM/Guidance on shared-prefix workloads including multi-turn chat
benchmarks.caveats: 2024 baseline comparison — vLLM has since shipped automatic prefix caching, narrowing the gap; gains depend heavily on prefix-sharing ratio of the workload.

benchmarks.benchmark: Provider cached-token pricing (verified from official docs, Aug 2026)
benchmarks.claim: Anthropic: cache reads 0.1x base input, writes 1.25x (5-min TTL) or 2x (1-hr TTL), min cacheable 512-4096 tokens by model, explicit cache_control breakpoints with 20-position prefix-hash lookback. OpenAI: cached input at 10% of base (90% discount) across GPT-5.x, automatic for prefixes >=1024 tokens, cache lifetime ~5-10 min (up to 1 hr); newer 5.6 models list explicit cache writes at 1.25x. Gemini: cached input ~10% of base (e.g. 2.5 Pro $0.125 vs $1.25/M), implicit caching default on 2.5+, explicit caches add storage of $1.00-$4.50 per M tokens per hour, min 2,048-4,096 tokens
benchmarks.caveats: Prices verified directly from provider docs on 2026-08-08 but change frequently. Economic implication: a stable memory prefix re-read every turn costs ~10% of face-value input pricing, which materially weakens the naive '90% token savings' pitch of memory layers when the counterfactual is cached long-context.

weaknesses: Hard write-time compression (fact/triple extraction) demonstrably loses information: the only independent cost-performance study found (arXiv:2603.04814) shows long-context GPT-5-mini with caching beats a fact-based memory system on factual recall on LongMemEval and LoCoMo — the two benchmarks memory vendors advertise wins on.

Vendor benchmark numbers in the memory-layer market are unreliable: the Zep-vs-Mem0 LoCoMo dispute (84% claimed -> 58.44% in Mem0's corrected eval -> 75.14% in Zep's rebuttal) shows both sides making methodology errors, and LoCoMo itself has documented speaker-misattribution and ambiguity flaws. Mem0's 2026 '92.5 LoCoMo' blog claim has no independent reproduction.

Headline '90% token savings' claims count only read-time tokens and ignore write-time cost: per-message LLM extraction and update-judgment calls are themselves token spend, and none of the vendor papers report total-cost-of-ownership including ingestion.

High compression ratios (20x LLMLingua, 26x gisting) are best-case: 20x holds only on redundant few-shot CoT prompts; task-agnostic compression of arbitrary context is 2-5x (LLMLingua-2's own framing). Soft-token methods (gisting, ICAE, AutoCompressor) require finetuning the serving model and cannot be used with closed API models where nearly all commercial memory layers operate.

Read-time compression and serving-side caching partially conflict: per-query dynamic compression/reranking produces a different prefix every call, breaking prefix-hash cache hits and forfeiting the 90% cached-token discount — almost no paper or vendor quantifies this interaction (arXiv:2603.04814 is the exception in even modeling caching).

Salience filtering and deduplication lack isolated measurements: no paper found reports precision/recall or compression contribution of dedup/salience stages alone; they are evaluated only as part of end-to-end systems.

Structured fact tables vs prose has thin direct literature: evidence is indirect (fact-based systems' benchmark results), and the one independent comparison suggests flat-typed facts only suit stable attributes, not contextual reasoning.

Compression accuracy gains (LongLLMLingua's +17-21% on NaturalQuestions) are partly an artifact of noisy retrieval — compression helps by deleting distractors; with clean retrieval the gain shrinks toward parity, so such numbers should not be read as free quality improvements.
pricing: Serving-side caching economics (verified from official docs 2026-08-08): Anthropic — cache reads 0.1x base input ($0.50/M on a $5/M model), 5-min-TTL writes 1.25x ($6.25/M), 1-hr-TTL writes 2x ($10/M), minimum cacheable prompt 512 tokens (Opus 5/Fable 5/Mythos 5) up to 4,096 on older models; explicit breakpoints, free refresh on reuse within TTL. OpenAI — cached input at 10% of base across GPT-5.x (GPT-5.4: $0.25 vs $2.50/M; GPT-5.6-sol: $0.50 vs $5.00/M), automatic for prefixes >=1024 tokens in 128-token increments, cache evicted after ~5-10 min idle (max ~1 hr); GPT-5.6 models additionally list explicit cache-write pricing at 1.25x. Google Gemini — cached input ~10% of base (2.5 Pro: $0.125 vs $1.25/M under 200K; 2.5 Flash: $0.03 vs $0.30/M), implicit caching on by default for 2.5+ models, explicit caches charge storage of $1.00/M tokens/hour (Flash-class) to $4.50/M tokens/hour (2.5 Pro), minimums 2,048-4,096 tokens by model. Memory-layer vendor pricing (Mem0/Zep/Letta SaaS tiers) was not verified in this pass and is excluded rather than repeated from secondary sources.

summary: The AI agent memory-layer market (Mem0, Zep, Letta, OpenAI's built-in memory) is being pulled toward compliance-grade features by three dated forcing functions: the EU AI Act's high-risk obligations — including Article 12 automatic lifetime event logging — which entered full application on 2 August 2026; US financial regulators (FINRA Notice 25-07, FINRA's 2026 Oversight Report) pressing firms to retain GenAI prompts/outputs as books-and-records; and HIPAA's audit-control and accounting-of-disclosures rules applying to vector stores holding PHI embeddings. "Auditable memory" is a defensible positioning because externalized, versioned memory converts GDPR right-to-erasure from an intractable machine-unlearning problem into a provable deletion operation, and incidents like the OpenAI/NYT preservation order (May–Sept 2025) and Garante fines (OpenAI €15M, Replika €5M) show retention/deletion of AI conversational data is now a litigated issue. However, the positioning is not open whitespace: Zep already ships SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA BAAs, bi-temporal fact invalidation with point-in-time queries, legal hold, audit logging, and BYOC deployment, so a new entrant must differentiate on deeper capabilities — per-decision reconstruction of exactly what an agent retrieved and knew, erasure with cryptographic proof and propagation to derived facts, and Article 12-shaped exportable logs — rather than on the word "auditable" alone.
architecture: This was market research, not a single-product teardown; what follows is the write/read architecture of each product's audit-relevant path, from primary docs. MEM0 (docs.mem0.ai): write path extracts facts from conversations into per-memory records; every mutation is logged as an ADD/UPDATE/DELETE event carrying old_memory and new_memory values, timestamps, user/agent/app identifiers, and the triggering conversation messages, retrievable via GET /v1/memories/{id}/history/ — a genuine per-memory audit trail, but scoped per memory ID, not a queryable point-in-time snapshot of the whole store; read path is vector retrieval (plus graph memory on Pro tier). ZEP (help.getzep.com/facts, getzep.com/security): write path ingests "episodes" (messages/business data) and extracts facts onto knowledge-graph edges stamped with four timestamps (created_at, valid_at, invalid_at, expired_at); superseded facts are invalidated, never deleted, preserving lineage; read path supports point-in-time queries ("what was true on date X") and every fact links back to its source episodes (retrieval provenance); governance layer adds ABAC, policy-driven retention with legal hold, and "detailed logs of every request and policy decision, ready for audit"; deployable as Cloud, Cloud+BYOK, or BYOC in customer VPC; open-source core is Graphiti. LETTA (docs.letta.com): agent-scoped core memory blocks plus archival memory in Postgres+pgvector; memory edits happen only through explicit tool calls (e.g., memory_replace), which makes changes traceable in principle, but no audit-log product, SSO/RBAC, or compliance certification is documented anywhere on letta.com or docs; self-hosted Docker surface is now deprecated in favor of Letta App Server. OPENAI (help.openai.com via search; openai.com/enterprise-privacy returned 403): ChatGPT Enterprise memory is a black box to the customer at retrieval time, but the Compliance Logs Platform exports conversations, files, GPT configs, and memories as immutable time-windowed JSONL with 30-day platform retention (customers must continuously export for longer holds); workspace admins can toggle memory and set retention; Enterprise Key Management (Dec 2025) allows customer-held keys; no provenance of which memories influenced a given response and no point-in-time reconstruction is offered.
token_strategy: Not the focus of this research and not independently verified here. Generically, all four products reduce tokens by injecting distilled memories/facts instead of replaying full conversation history; Zep markets sub-200ms p95 retrieval of a compact context block assembled from its graph (vendor claim on getzep.com). No token-reduction numbers were verified from primary benchmarks in this session; treat all such figures (e.g., Mem0's ~90%-token-saving marketing) as vendor claims unless separately validated.

benchmarks.benchmark: Gartner AI governance platform spending forecast
benchmarks.claim: AI governance platform spend reaches $492M in 2026 and surpasses $1B by 2030; Gartner launched its first Magic Quadrant for AI Governance Platforms (Feb 2026)
benchmarks.caveats: Analyst forecast, not observed spend; small in absolute terms next to Gartner's $64B 2026 AI platforms/models forecast — governance is a budget line, not yet a large market. Secondary sources claiming governance is 8-12% of enterprise AI budgets could not be traced to a primary source.

benchmarks.benchmark: EU AI Act Article 12 logging mandate
benchmarks.claim: High-risk AI systems must technically allow automatic recording of events (logs) over the system lifetime; full application from 2 Aug 2026; providers/deployers must keep logs at least six months (Arts. 19, 26); penalties up to EUR 15M or 3% of worldwide turnover for this class of violation
benchmarks.caveats: Article 12 text verified by direct fetch; the six-month retention floor and penalty tiers come from cross-referenced articles reported in secondary sources, not fetched verbatim. Applies only to systems classified high-risk under Annex III — most agent-memory deployments are not automatically high-risk.

benchmarks.claim: Sub-200ms p95 retrieval at enterprise scale on the Context Graph Engine
benchmarks.caveats: Vendor claim; no independent benchmark found.

benchmarks.claim: SOC 2 Type I certified, HIPAA-ready, SOC 2 Type II audit in progress
benchmarks.caveats: Trust center page is JS-rendered and returned no verifiable content to a direct fetch; status is drawn from search-indexed copies of mem0.ai/security. HIPAA 'ready' is self-attested, not a certification; weaker than Zep's audited SOC 2 Type II + BAA.

pricing: Mem0 (mem0.ai/pricing, fetched): Hobby free (10K add / 1K retrieval requests/mo); Starter $19/mo; Pro $249/mo (500K add / 50K retrieval, graph memory, consolidation); Enterprise custom — and notably audit logs, on-prem deployment, SSO, and SLAs are gated to the Enterprise tier. Zep (getzep.com/pricing, fetched): Free (10K credits/mo); Flex $125/mo (50K credits, 1-day API log retention); Flex Plus $375/mo (200K credits, 7-day log retention); "Emerging Companies" $13K/yr; Enterprise custom — SOC 2 Type II/HIPAA BAA coverage, 1-year audit and API log retention, BYOK/BYOC, and EU DPAs are Enterprise-gated. Letta: open source (Apache 2.0) self-hosted free; no cloud pricing published on letta.com. OpenAI: ChatGPT Enterprise pricing unpublished (sales-gated); Compliance Logs Platform and data residency are Enterprise features, residency sales-gated on new workspaces/projects. Pattern: in every commercial product, the audit/residency features an "auditable memory" pitch targets are enterprise-tier upsells, not defaults.
weaknesses: The positioning's flagship claim is already partially occupied: Zep ships SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA BAAs, bi-temporal fact invalidation, point-in-time queries, episode-level provenance, legal hold, ABAC, request-level audit logs, and BYOC today — an 'auditable memory' entrant competes with an incumbent's shipped feature list, not a gap.

The addressable governance budget is small: Gartner's $492M 2026 forecast for all AI governance platforms is under 1% of its $64B AI platforms forecast; audit features today monetize as enterprise-tier upsells on memory products, not as standalone purchases.

Regulatory hooks are real but not yet prescriptive for memory layers specifically: SEC/FINRA have issued no definitive rule that AI prompts/outputs are 17a-4 records (firms make risk-based judgments per FINRA Notice 25-07 and the ABA analysis), and EU AI Act Article 12 binds only high-risk Annex III systems — many agent-memory deployments fall outside it.

Verification gaps found during research: Mem0's trust center (trust.mem0.ai) rendered no machine-readable content, its HIPAA posture is self-attested, and SOC 2 Type II was still in progress per secondary sources; Letta has no discoverable compliance page, audit-log product, SSO/RBAC, or certification at all — claims about its 'auditable' tool-call memory edits are architectural potential, not product; OpenAI's enterprise-privacy and compliance-platform pages 403'd direct fetches, so its capabilities are sourced from help-center content surfaced via search, not verified verbatim.

Point-in-time reconstruction remains partially unsolved even at Zep: fact-level history exists, but no vendor demonstrates reconstruction of the full retrieval context behind a specific past agent decision ('what did the agent know and retrieve when it did X'), and none offers erasure with proof that propagates to derived/consolidated facts — that narrower claim is the actual whitespace, and it is harder to build than an audit log.

Demand-side evidence is strongest for logging/retention (OpenAI-NYT preservation order, FINRA 2026 report, COSO Feb 2026 GenAI internal-control guidance, RFP questionnaire blocks) but that demand is being met by export/e-discovery tooling (OpenAI Compliance Logs Platform, Smarsh-style archiving) as much as by memory-layer-native auditability — buyers may satisfy auditors at the log-export layer without switching memory vendors.
